chunk_findings.detail:
`_FRONT` is compiled without `re.DOTALL`, so `(.*?)` cannot cross a newline. The regex therefore only matches front matter that is a *single* line (`---\nkey: val\n---`), which no real Claude/Cursor file has. Feed the canonical SKILL.md:

```
---
name: deploy-helper
description: Deploy the service to staging
---
# Deploy
```

`_FRONT.match` fails (after `---\n` the lazy group can only consume `name: deploy-helper`, then `\r?\n`, then the literal `---` must match at `description: ...` and does not; the group can't grow past the newline). `_frontmatter` returns `({}, text)`, `body` is the *whole* file, and `_first_line(body)` returns the delimiter — so `desc == "---"` and `line()` renders `- skill **deploy-helper** — --- (`.claude/skills/deploy-helper/SKILL.md`)`, i.e. the brief prints `---` as the description for essentially every skill/command/rule. It also silently discards a front-matter `name`, forcing the directory/file-name fallback. The tell is the loop `for line in m.group(1).splitlines()` inside `_frontmatter`: `group(1)` can never contain a newline, so that loop is unreachable — the regex was meant to carry `re.S` (as `_DDFLOW_BLOCK` below it does). Same path affects `.cursor/rules/*.mdc` and `.clinerules/**.md`, which also use multi-line `description:` front matter.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/skills.py:19 (`_FRONT` / `_frontmatter`)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_entry` routes file text through `_frontmatter()` before deriving a description, but `_agent_file` does not: it computes `_first_line(text)` on the raw file (only the ddflow block is stripped). Given an `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` that starts with YAML frontmatter, e.g.:

```
---
name: agents
description: project conventions
---

# Agents
...
```

`_first_line` walks the lines, and the first non-empty `strip().lstrip("#").strip()` result is the literal `---`, so the brief renders `- rule **AGENTS.md** — --- (`AGENTS.md`)`. The real description ("project conventions") is neither shown nor included in the BM25 text (the raw frontmatter delimiters and YAML keys/values are, instead, ranked). `_entry` avoids this for skills/commands/rules; `_agent_file` does not, so any frontmatter in these two files yields a garbage description plus polluted ranking tokens.

chunk_findings.detail: The change removes the public name `workflow_state` from `ddflow.api` by renaming the alias to `workflow_overview`, both in the import and in `__all__`. The intent text still describes the feature as `workflow_state` ("rewrite workflow_state on the real State model"), and the README table in this same diff advertises the MCP tool as `ddflow_workflow_state` and the CLI as `ddflow workflow state` — but the API no longer exports anything named `workflow_state`. Concretely: any code doing `from ddflow.api import workflow_state` (including whatever registers the `ddflow_workflow_state` MCP tool, and any test/user following the documented name) now raises `ImportError: cannot import name 'workflow_state' from 'ddflow.api'`, since `__all__` only lists `workflow_overview`. If the rename is intentional, the README/MCP-name references must be updated to `_overview`; if it is not, the export name should stay `workflow_state` (e.g. alias the function to a non-colliding internal name while keeping the public binding), because the submodule `ddflow.api.workflow_state` will otherwise shadow the function attribute on `ddflow.api` once that submodule is imported.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/__init__.py:175 (import/`__all__` rename)

chunk_findings.detail: `_over_limits` is invoked unconditionally at the top of `rule_add`, before the code decides whether it is creating a *new* rule or updating an *existing* one. The update path is real: `apply_rule_update` (line ~288) branches on `existing` and calls `storage.update(rule.id, ...)` for a rule whose id already exists, and `rule_add` reaches it via `apply_rule_update(repo, rule, agent=agent, operation="created")`. The last check in `_over_limits`, `len(RulesStorage(repo).list()) >= cfg.rules.max_rules`, counts the current ruleset including the very rule being edited. Concrete failure: project configured with `rules.max_rules = 10` and 10 rules already stored; the caller invokes `rule_add` with an already-existing rule id to change its title/tags. `_over_limits` sees `len(...) == 10 >= 10` and returns `O.refused("rule.added", "the project already has rules.max_rules (10) rules")`, so a modification of an existing rule is rejected even though the rule count would not increase. The count check needs to exclude the rule being updated (or `_over_limits` must only run on the genuine add path).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/rules.py:_over_limits (called from rule_add)

chunk_findings.detail: At that point `verb = a.rule_cmd or "list"`. Every value of `rule_cmd` that is `list`/`search`/`show`/`remove`/`edit` has already returned earlier in `cmd_rule`, so the only reachable `verb` here is `"add"` (i.e. a user running `ddflow rule add --check ...`). `_emit` in JSON mode does `out.body(_PAYLOADS[verb])`, i.e. `_PAYLOADS["add"] == ("id", "candidates")`. But this branch's outcome comes from `rule_dedup_check_dry_run`, not `rule_add`: its data is a dedup-check result whose only relevant field is `candidates` (the non-JSON path itself only reads `out.data.get("candidates", [])`). There is no top-level `id` on a dry-run result, and `_PAYLOADS` has no entry for the dry-run response shape at all. So `ddflow rule add --check "<text>" --json` projects through the wrong payload: it either raises a `KeyError`/lookup failure inside `Outcome.body` (if the projection requires the declared keys to exist) or silently emits a fabricated `"id": null` alongside `candidates`. Either way the JSON output of the check is wrong; the projection for the check path should be the dedup-check body (`candidates`), not the add body.

chunk_findings.detail: The handler for the `ddflow_workflow_state` tool was changed from invoking `_api().workflow_state(repo, agent)` to `_api().workflow_overview(repo, agent)`, while the tool's public name, the surrounding schema, and the change's stated intent ("rewrite workflow_state on the real State model") all continue to reference `workflow_state`. If the api layer exposes `workflow_state` (as it did before and as the intent implies — the intent says the existing function is *rewritten*, not renamed), then any call to `ddflow_workflow_state` with empty arguments executes `_api().workflow_overview(...)`, which raises `AttributeError` because the attribute does not exist on the api object, causing the tool to fail for every caller. The rename therefore needs to be confirmed to exist in the api module (or the lambda reverted to `workflow_state`); as written, the tool name and the invoked method are not the same symbol.

chunk_findings.detail: The re-export was renamed with no back-compat alias: `from .workflow_state import workflow_state as workflow_overview` and `__all__` now lists `"workflow_overview"`. The concrete failure: any existing caller doing `from ddflow.api import workflow_state` (or `ddflow.api.workflow_state`) now raises `ImportError: cannot import name 'workflow_state'`, even though the change's stated intent is only to "rewrite workflow_state on the real State model", not to rename it. The mismatch is corroborated by the same diff's README table, which still documents the tool as `ddflow_workflow_state` (and CLI `ddflow workflow state`); if MCP tool registration is driven by the names in `ddflow.api.__all__`, the registered tool becomes `ddflow_workflow_overview` and no longer matches the documented `ddflow_workflow_state`. Either the old name must remain as an alias, or the README/MCP name must be updated in lockstep.

chunk_findings.detail: `_over_limits` is invoked unconditionally at the start of `rule_add`, before the `if not check_dedup: return apply_rule_update(...)` branch. But `rule_add` is also the path used to *update* an existing rule (the dedup "extends <id>" flow, and any call with `check_dedup=False` that resolves to an existing rule via `apply_rule_update`). The limit check uses `len(RulesStorage(repo).list()) >= cfg.rules.max_rules` without excluding the rule being updated, so once the project already holds exactly `rules.max_rules` rules, every subsequent `rule_add` is refused with `"the project already has rules.max_rules (N) rules"` — even when it would merely rewrite an existing rule and the total count would not increase. Demonstrating input: a project at the configured cap, then `rule_add(repo, rule=<same id/existing rule>, agent=..., check_dedup=False)`; `_over_limits` returns the refusal before `apply_rule_update` runs, so legitimately extending/updating a rule is impossible at the cap. The docstring states the intent is to refuse a *new* rule, so the check should either run only for genuinely new rules or compare against `len(list()) - 1` when the target rule already exists.

chunk_findings.detail: The `check` path calls `_emit(c, out, verb, ...)`, and `_emit` does `_PAYLOADS[verb]` whenever `c.json` is set. But `_PAYLOADS` only has entries for `list`, `search`, `add`, `edit`, `remove`, `show` — there is no `"check"` key, and the dispatch never reassigns `verb` from `"check"` to anything else (the check branch is reached through the fall-through `if a.check:` after the `list/search/show/remove/edit` checks, with `verb = a.rule_cmd or "list"`). So running the check subcommand with JSON output, e.g. `ddflow rule check "<content>" --json`, reaches `print(json.dumps(out.body(_PAYLOADS["check"]), ...))` and raises `KeyError: 'check'` instead of emitting the candidates. Even under the alternative reading where `check` is a `--check` flag on `add` (so `verb == "add"`), the projection `("id", "candidates")` still asks the dry-run result for an `id`, which a dry run that creates no rule does not have. Either way the check path's `_emit` call cannot produce valid JSON, because it is the one branch whose verb/projection was never added to `_PAYLOADS`.

chunk_findings.detail: The old renderer read optional fields defensively — `overview.get('workflow_diagram', '(unavailable)')` and `bug.get("fix_task")` in both the open and in-progress bug loops — which is direct evidence that `workflow_state` data can omit these keys or carry them as `None`. The new code indexes them directly: `o["workflow_diagram"]` is inserted into the `lines` list before `"\n".join(lines)`, and the bugs loop evaluates `b["fix_task"]` inside the comprehension. Given a repository whose state payload has no diagram (the exact case the old `'(unavailable)'` default covered), `o["workflow_diagram"]` raises `KeyError` and the whole `ddflow workflow state` text command aborts instead of degrading; likewise a bug entry without a `fix_task` key raises `KeyError` at `b["fix_task"]` rather than printing `[no fix task]`. The JSON branch is unaffected, so `-json` and text mode now diverge in robustness for the same data. (Confidence note: if the rewritten API is guaranteed to always emit these keys with string/`None` values, this is moot — but the removed defaults are the only signal available in the diff, and they point the other way.)

chunk_findings.detail: The diff renames the public export `workflow_state` to `workflow_overview`, but the README table entry added in this same change documents the MCP tool as `ddflow_workflow_state`. These two names no longer agree. If the MCP tool surface is derived from the symbol exported here (the conventional pattern for this package: `ddflow_workflow`, `ddflow_rule_*`, etc. all mirror their `ddflow.api` export names), then the tool exposed to clients will be `ddflow_workflow_overview`, and any caller following the README and invoking `ddflow_workflow_state` will fail with an unknown-tool error. Symmetrically, any existing Python code doing `from ddflow.api import workflow_state` (the previous public name) now raises `ImportError` because the name is gone from both the import and `__all__`. Either the README should say `ddflow_workflow_overview`, or the export should keep the `workflow_state` name (or expose both via an alias).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/__init__.py:175 (workflow_overview)

chunk_findings.detail: `_over_limits` refuses whenever `len(RulesStorage(repo).list()) >= cfg.rules.max_rules`, without distinguishing a genuinely new rule from an update to an existing one. But `rule_add` delegates to `apply_rule_update`, which explicitly has an `if existing: storage.update(...)` branch for rules whose `id` already exists — so `rule_add` is used both to add and to update. Given a project that already holds exactly `rules.max_rules` rules, calling `rule_add` with an existing rule's id to change its content (or its globs/priority) now returns `O.refused("rule.added", "the project already has rules.max_rules (N) rules")` before the update path is ever reached, even though no new rule is being created and the rule count is unchanged. This contradicts the docstring's stated intent ("Refuse a **new** rule that breaks the project's [rules] limits") and blocks all edits once the project is at the cap. The count check needs to exempt the rule being updated (e.g. only apply when `rule.id` is not already present, or compare `count > max - 1` only for additions).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/rules.py `_over_limits` / `rule_add`

chunk_findings.detail:
The parent `rule` parser calls `set_defaults(..., scope="")`. In argparse, `parse_known_args` pre-populates the namespace with the parent's `set_defaults` values before dispatching into a subparser, and the subparser only applies an action's default when the attribute is *not already present* (`if not hasattr(namespace, action.dest)`). Because `namespace.scope` already exists (as `""`), the subparsers' own declared defaults are silently skipped:

- `ddflow rule add --id X --title Y` (no `--scope`): the `add` parser declares `--scope` with `default="project"`, but that default is never applied; `args.scope` ends up `""` instead of `"project"`.
- `ddflow rule edit <id> --title Z` (no `--scope`): the `edit` parser declares `--scope` with `default=None` to mean "leave unchanged"; it is likewise skipped, so `args.scope` is `""` rather than `None`, which can cause an edit to overwrite the stored scope with an empty string.

The parent's `tag=""`/`scope=""` defaults are only needed for the bare `rule` → `list` case; they are redundant for the `list`/`search` subparsers (which already declare the same defaults) and actively clobber the `add`/`edit` defaults. Note `--tags` (plural) is unaffected, so `scope` is the only colliding dest.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/cli.py:~992 (`ru.set_defaults(fn=cmd_rule, rule_cmd="list", tag="", scope="")`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The `add` verb declares its wire projection as `("id", "candidates")` in `_PAYLOADS`, and the module docstring promises the CLI and the MCP tools return the *same wire bodies* (the candidates are exactly what a caller needs in order to answer the dedup question via `--new/--extends/--duplicate-of/--related`). But on the dedup-conflict path the candidates are dropped before any body is emitted:

```python
if out.exit != 0 and out.data.get("candidates"):
    print(out.reason, file=sys.stderr)
    return out.exit
return _emit(c, out, verb, f"added rule {a.id}")
```

The guard `out.exit != 0 and out.data.get("candidates")` is precisely the "this failure carries candidates" case, and it prints only `out.reason` to stderr and returns, so nothing is written to stdout. Even if the guard were removed, `_emit`'s own `if out.exit == FAIL: ...; return FAIL` branch would short-circuit and never call `out.body(_PAYLOADS["add"])`. Concrete input: `ddflow rule add --json id=x title=t content="<content that duplicates an existing rule>"` with no dedup-answer flag. `rule_add` returns a nonzero Outcome whose `data` contains `candidates`; the CLI exits nonzero with empty stdout, so a JSON/MCP-style consumer never receives the candidate list it needs to retry with an answer — the exact payload the `("id", "candidates")` projection exists to carry. Human mode has the same gap (only `out.reason` is shown), so the add-with-dedup flow can only be completed by first running the separate `--check` dry run, which contradicts the stated parity with the MCP tool.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/rules.py:119 (cmd_rule, "add" branch)

chunk_findings.detail: The rename `from .workflow_state import workflow_state as workflow_overview` does not just add a new name — it changes what the existing package attribute `ddflow.api.workflow_state` refers to. Importing the submodule always sets the parent package attribute to the *module object* (`setattr(ddflow.api, "workflow_state", <module>)`), and the old code immediately rebinding the name to the callable is what made `ddflow.api.workflow_state` be the function. After this change nothing rebinds that name, so `ddflow.api.workflow_state` is now the module. Concretely, `from ddflow.api import workflow_state; workflow_state(...)` (or `ddflow.api.workflow_state(...)`) raises `TypeError: 'module' object is not callable`, whereas it previously invoked the function. Any consumer that was not renamed in the same commit (e.g. a CLI `workflow state` command or MCP registration that imports the symbol by its old name) now fails at the call site instead of failing to import, i.e. it silently degrades from "attribute error/import error" to a runtime TypeError. If the rename was meant to be additive, a `workflow_state = workflow_overview` alias was required.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/__init__.py:175

chunk_findings.detail: The README table still documents the MCP tool as `ddflow_workflow_state` and the CLI as `ddflow workflow state`, but the exported symbol is now `workflow_overview` (and `__all__` no longer contains `workflow_state`). If the MCP tool surface is derived from `ddflow.api.__all__`/the exported callable names, the advertised tool `ddflow_workflow_state` no longer exists and is replaced by `ddflow_workflow_overview`; a caller following the README gets an unknown-tool error. Either the export or the documented name is wrong — the change updates one and not the other.
chunk_findings.title: README.md:163 vs ddflow/api/__init__.py:175,301

chunk_findings.detail: The `max_rules` guard is evaluated unconditionally at the top of `rule_add`, before `rule_add` decides whether the operation is an insert or an update. `len(RulesStorage(repo).list())` counts the rule that is already on disk, so when a project is exactly at `rules.max_rules`, the guard fires even when `rule.id` is the id of an existing rule that would be *updated* rather than added — the rule count would not increase. Concretely, with 5 rules on disk and `rules.max_rules == 5`, calling `rule_add(repo, <rule with id of existing rule>, check_dedup=False)` takes the `if not check_dedup: return apply_rule_update(...)` path shown at the same hunk, whose `if existing:` branch would have performed `storage.update(rule.id, ...)`; instead `_over_limits` returns `O.refused("rule.added", "the project already has rules.max_rules (5) rules")`. This makes the "extends <existing id>" flow (the very remedy offered by the duplicate-refusal message, which asks the user to answer `extends {candidates[0]['id']}`) unusable once the project is at capacity: you can never merge into or edit an existing rule while at the limit, even though no new rule is created and the count is unchanged. The correct count for the guard would have to exclude the rule being updated (or the guard would need to run only on the insert branch), otherwise a full project is permanently frozen against updates.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/rules.py:_over_limits (max_rules branch)

Concretely: agent B holds `refs/ddflow/claims/X` with `expires = now + 3600`. Agent A calls `take(...)`; A's root-commit push is correctly rejected as non-fast-forward; `_remote_sha` succeeds and returns B's sha `cur`; then `_read` runs `git fetch --no-tags <remote> refs/ddflow/claims/X`, which times out (the `TIMEOUT_S = 30` fetch is a data-transfer, and can time out on a slow/lossy link even though the earlier small `ls-remote` succeeded) and returns `("", 0.0)`. Back in `take`, `owner == holder` is false but `lapses <= time.time()` is `0.0 <= time.time()` → true, so A issues `git push --force-with-lease=<ref>:<cur>` at the sha B still holds, that push succeeds, and A returns `Result("ok", ...)` while B's live, unexpired claim is silently overwritten. This directly contradicts the module docstring ("`unavailable` ... is never treated as success"): a fetch failure or a claim message that `_parse` cannot read (missing/malformed `expires:` line ⇒ `0.0`) is treated as "expired" and grants the lock. chunk_findings.detail:
`_remote_drop(log, item_id)` is invoked unconditionally whenever the *local* transition succeeds in `release()` (line ~572) and `expire()` (line ~596), and it takes only `item_id` — no holder, no expected-value. It therefore cannot be a compare-and-swap: whatever ref `CR.drop` finds at `refs/ddflow/claims/<id>` is deleted, even if it is currently held by *another clone*.

Concrete failure: clone A has a lease record for X in remote mode. A crashes/the lease lapses, A's remote TTL elapses, and clone B wins the CAS and now legitimately holds X (remote ref written, B's local lease acquired). A's recovery still has the stale X lease entry and calls `expire(log, "X")` (or an operator calls `release(log, "X")`; release explicitly does not require the caller to be the holder). `_transition` succeeds locally, `done` is True, and `_remote_drop` deletes B's freshly-written ref. B continues to renew/heartbeat locally believing it holds X, while clone C can now `_remote_take` X successfully — two clones hold the same item, exactly the split-brain `[flow].claims = "remote"` exists to prevent. The only "protection" is the sentence "a ref we fail to delete lapses" — but here the delete *succeeds*, and it succeeds against the wrong owner. The drop must be conditional on the ref still naming the same holder the local lease transitioned (or on `CR.drop` taking the expected holder so it can CAS-delete), otherwise `expire`/`release` of a lapsed lease silently evicts the current remote holder.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_read()` collapses every failure to read the existing claim into the value `("", 0.0)`:

```python
def _read(...):
    got = _run(root, "fetch", "--no-tags", remote, ref)
    if got is None or isinstance(got, OSError) or not got.ok:
        return "", 0.0          # <-- "could not read" is encoded as "expired"
    ...
```

`take()` then does `if owner == holder or lapses <= time.time():` and treats `lapses == 0.0` as a lapsed claim, so it force-with-leases over the existing ref even though nothing is known about its expiry:

```python
owner, lapses = _read(root, remote, ref, cur)
if owner == holder or lapses <= time.time():      # 0.0 <= now  -> True
    swapped = _run(root, ..., f"--force-with-lease={ref}:{cur}", remote, f"{sha}:{ref}")
```

Concrete failure: agent A holds `refs/ddflow/claims/x` with `expires` one hour in the future. Agent B runs `take`. `ls-remote` succeeds and returns A's `cur` sha, but the subsequent `fetch`/`cat-file` for that sha fails transiently (flaky link, server hiccup, or `fetch` storing a different sha so `cat-file commit cur` misses). `_read` returns `("", 0.0)`, `0.0 <= time.time()` is true, and B's `--force-with-lease=x:<cur>` still passes because the remote ref *is* `cur`. B's push succeeds and `take` returns `Result("ok", ...)`, so both A and B now believe they own `x` — exactly the mutual exclusion this module exists to provide. Note the asymmetry: `renew` uses the same `_read`, but there an unreadable ref yields `owner != holder` and fails safe (`held`), so the bug is specific to `take`.

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring asserts "unsafe characters become `%XX`, so ids stay distinct", but `f"%{ord(m.group()):02x}"` emits a *variable-width* hex escape for code points ≥ 0x100, which is not injective. Concrete input: item `"\u0100"` (single char U+0100) → `"%100"`; item `"\x100"` (parsed by Python as the two chars `"\x10"` + `"0"`) → `"%10"` + `"0"` = `"%100"`. Two distinct item ids therefore map to the same `refs/ddflow/claims/%100`, so claiming one item falsely blocks the other. The mapping is injective only for code points below 0x100 (where `%` is itself escaped to `%25`).

chunk_findings.detail:
`_remote_renew` discards `CR.renew`'s result, and both of its callers treat the call as infallible. `CR.take` demonstrably returns a status object (`got.status`/`got.holder`/`got.expires`/`got.detail`) that the take path inspects and refuses on; `CR.renew` is the symmetric operation and its outcome is thrown away.

Concrete failure: `[flow].claims = "remote"`, two clones A and B. A claims item X — `_remote_take` creates `refs/ddflow/claims/X` with `expires = now + ttl`, and A appends its local lease. A's heartbeat later runs `renew`, which first succeeds locally (`_renew_local` returns True), then calls `_remote_renew`. The remote is transiently unreachable, or the ref has already lapsed and been re-taken, so `CR.renew` reports a refusal/failure — and nothing happens: no exception, no logging, `ok=True` is returned to the caller, and A keeps renewing its *local* lease forever. Once the remote ref's expiry passes, B's `_remote_take` sees the ref as free and succeeds, so A and B both work X — exactly the split-brain the setting exists to prevent, with A never being told. The same silent path is taken at `leases.py:240` when the holder re-claims an item it already holds.

The asymmetry is the defect: a claim that cannot reach the remote is refused, but a heartbeat that cannot reach (or has lost) the remote is treated as success. If the freshest remote-read status is `held`/`detail` for a different holder, the local renewal should at minimum refuse or surface it the way `_remote_take` does. Note also that this broken invariant ("I hold the local lease ⇒ I hold the remote ref") is what makes the unconditional, holder-less `CR.drop(log.root, cfg.flow.remote, item_id)` in `_remote_drop` unsafe: after A's remote renew has silently lapsed and B has taken the ref, A's eventual `release`/`expire` deletes *B's* valid claim ref, letting a third clone take X while B believes it holds it.

chunk_findings.detail:
The remote claim's expiry and the local lease's expiry are now computed from two different clocks, and the remote one is always the earlier. `acquire` evaluates `time.time()` *before* calling `_remote_take`, and `_remote_take` writes the remote ref with `now + cfg.lease.ttl_s`. `_acquire_locked` then captures its own `now = time.time()` *after* `_remote_take` has returned (the docstring itself says this can be up to six git subprocesses at 30 s each, i.e. ~180 s, plus however long the process then waits for the log append lock) and records the local lease with that later `now`. So the remote ref always expires `take_duration + lock_wait` before the local lease does.

Concrete case: `[flow].claims = "remote"`, `lease.ttl_s = 300`, and a `_remote_take` that takes 120 s. The remote ref is written with expiry `t+300`; `_acquire_locked` records the local lease with expiry `t+120+300 = t+420`. At `t+310` the remote ref is expired but the first clone's local lease is still valid (and its grace period hasn't even started). chunk_findings.detail:
`_read()` collapses every failure to read the existing claim into the value `("", 0.0)`:

```python
def _read(...):
    got = _run(root, "fetch", "--no-tags", remote, ref)
    if got is None or isinstance(got, OSError) or not got.ok:
        return "", 0.0          # <-- "could not read" is encoded as "expired"
    ...
```

`take()` then does `if owner == holder or lapses <= time.time():` and treats `lapses == 0.0` as a lapsed claim, so it force-with-leases over the existing ref even though nothing is known about its expiry:

```python
owner, lapses = _read(root, remote, ref, cur)
if owner == holder or lapses <= time.time():      # 0.0 <= now  -> True
    swapped = _run(root, ..., f"--force-with-lease={ref}:{cur}", remote, f"{sha}:{ref}")
```

Concrete failure: agent A holds `refs/ddflow/claims/x` with `expires` one hour in the future. Agent B runs `take`. `ls-remote` succeeds and returns A's `cur` sha, but the subsequent `fetch`/`cat-file` for that sha fails transiently (flaky link, server hiccup, or `fetch` storing a different sha so `cat-file commit cur` misses). `_read` returns `("", 0.0)`, `0.0 <= time.time()` is true, and B's `--force-with-lease=x:<cur>` still passes because the remote ref *is* `cur`. B's push succeeds and `take` returns `Result("ok", ...)`, so both A and B now believe they own `x` — exactly the mutual exclusion this module exists to provide. Note the asymmetry: `renew` uses the same `_read`, but there an unreadable ref yields `owner != holder` and fails safe (`held`), so the bug is specific to `take`.

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring asserts "unsafe characters become `%XX`, so ids stay distinct", but `f"%{ord(m.group()):02x}"` emits a *variable-width* hex escape for code points ≥ 0x100, which is not injective. Concrete input: item `"\u0100"` (single char U+0100) → `"%100"`; item `"\x100"` (parsed by Python as the two chars `"\x10"` + `"0"`) → `"%10"` + `"0"` = `"%100"`. Two distinct item ids therefore map to the same `refs/ddflow/claims/%100`, so claiming one item falsely blocks the other. The mapping is injective only for code points below 0x100 (where `%` is itself escaped to `%25`).

chunk_findings.detail:
`_remote_renew` discards `CR.renew`'s result, and both of its callers treat the call as infallible. `CR.take` demonstrably returns a status object (`got.status`/`got.holder`/`got.expires`/`got.detail`) that the take path inspects and refuses on; `CR.renew` is the symmetric operation and its outcome is thrown away.

Concrete failure: `[flow].claims = "remote"`, two clones A and B. A claims item X — `_remote_take` creates `refs/ddflow/claims/X` with `expires = now + ttl`, and A appends its local lease. A's heartbeat later runs `renew`, which first succeeds locally (`_renew_local` returns True), then calls `_remote_renew`. The remote is transiently unreachable, or the ref has already lapsed and been re-taken, so `CR.renew` reports a refusal/failure — and nothing happens: no exception, no logging, `ok=True` is returned to the caller, and A keeps renewing its *local* lease forever. Once the remote ref's expiry passes, B's `_remote_take` sees the ref as free and succeeds, so A and B both work X — exactly the split-brain the setting exists to prevent, with A never being told. The same silent path is taken at `leases.py:240` when the holder re-claims an item it already holds.

The asymmetry is the defect: a claim that cannot reach the remote is refused, but a heartbeat that cannot reach (or has lost) the remote is treated as success. If the freshest remote-read status is `held`/`detail` for a different holder, the local renewal should at minimum refuse or surface it the way `_remote_take` does. Note also that this broken invariant ("I hold the local lease ⇒ I hold the remote ref") is what makes the unconditional, holder-less `CR.drop(log.root, cfg.flow.remote, item_id)` in `_remote_drop` unsafe: after A's remote renew has silently lapsed and B has taken the ref, A's eventual `release`/`expire` deletes *B's* valid claim ref, letting a third clone take X while B believes it holds it.

chunk_findings.detail: `ref_name` now encodes each character with `c.encode("utf-8")`, which raises `UnicodeEncodeError` for a lone surrogate (Python's default error handler is `strict`, and lone surrogates are not encodable). The previous implementation used `ord(m.group())` and therefore produced a string for *any* input. Lone surrogates are not hypothetical: `sys.argv` is decoded with `os.fsdecode`/surrogateescape on Unix, so an item id passed as a non-UTF-8 byte argument (e.g. `ddflow claim $'\xff'`) becomes `'\udcff'`; likewise filesystem-derived ids via `surrogateescape`. Calling `ref_name('\udcff')` raises `UnicodeEncodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't encode character '\udcff'` instead of returning `refs/ddflow/claims/%dcff`. In `take`/`renew` the `ref = ref_name(item)` call sits *outside* the `try` blocks (only `_make_commit` is guarded), so this propagates as an unhandled exception/crash rather than a `Result`, whereas the old code handled the same input fine. The fix would be to encode with `errors="surrogatepass"` (or otherwise handle unencodable code points) to preserve the "any item id maps to a valid ref" guarantee.

chunk_findings.detail: `_transition` now returns `not _remote_renew(log, Config.load(log.root), item_id, holder or log.agent_id, ...)` on success, and `release` assigns that to `done` (`done = _transition(log, item_id, ...)`). The value `_remote_renew` returns is the identity of whoever holds the remote claim *instead of us*, so `_transition` now reports "we still hold the remote claim" rather than "the local transition was recorded". `release` is the operator-releasing-a-crashed-agent's-lease path documented as the normal case: release computes `by = holder or log.agent_id` (the operator) and the owner is only captured through the `owner` callback inside `_transition`, so the renew runs under the actor/`log.agent_id`, not the crashed agent who actually holds the ref. Concretely: clone A holds the local lease for item X and its ref is held by that same crashed agent's identity; an operator on clone A releases it. `CR.renew` for the operator sees the ref held by the other holder, `_remote_renew` returns that holder (truthy), `_transition` returns `False`, and `release` reports the release as not done even though `lease.released` was appended locally; if release gates its `_remote_drop` on `done`, the remote claim is never given back and stays live until its TTL. Before this change the renew result was discarded and `_transition` returned the local `ok`, so release's result did not depend on a remote renew attempted under the wrong holder. (Additionally, renewing at all on a release only makes sense if the ref is then dropped unconditionally, which the new `done` gate can now prevent.)

chunk_findings.detail: The encoder is not injective for code points above U+00FF, because `f"%{ord(c):02x}"` emits more than two hex digits and is not prefixed by a length. `ord("€") = 0x20AC` ⇒ `%20ac`, while `" ac"` (space + `a` + `c`) ⇒ `%20` + `ac` ⇒ `%20ac` as well. Any escaping scheme that must be collision-free needs a delimiter/prefix (e.g. encode the encoded byte length, or also escape a separator) so the escape sequence cannot be produced by a literal character.

chunk_findings.detail: `drop` never checks who holds the ref: it reads the current sha and force-with-lease deletes whatever is at that sha. chunk_findings.detail:
When `cfg.flow.claims == "remote"` and `_holds_live(...)` is true, `acquire` now only calls `_remote_renew(...)` and never `_remote_take(...)`. But `_holds_live` consults **local** state only:

```python
it = _decide_from(log)[0].items.get(item_id)
lease = it.lease if it else None
return bool(lease and lease.holder == holder and not lease.expired(...))
```

So it can be true while the remote claim is gone. That is exactly the state the change's own comment describes for an outage ("it lapses at its expiry and the next heartbeat re-takes it"): the heartbeat keeps extending the local lease while `_remote_renew` cannot reach the remote, so the remote claim lapses and re-taking is a separate step. Once the remote is reachable again, calling `acquire(X)` finds `_holds_live` true, `_remote_renew` finds no live claim of ours to extend and returns falsy (no "lost" holder), and the code falls through to `_acquire_locked` and reports success *without ever re-establishing the remote claim*. Previously `acquire` unconditionally did `took = _remote_take(...)`, which claims an absent remote lease. Concrete input: `claims="remote"`, local lease for `X` held by us and unexpired, remote lease absent (but remote reachable) → `acquire(X)` returns success with no remote lock held; a second agent can then take the free remote lease and also succeed, so both agents believe they own `X`. The routing branch needs to distinguish "remote still ours" from "remote absent" (e.g., still call `_remote_take` when the renew finds nothing, only tolerating an unreachable-remote error).

chunk_findings.detail: `_read` collapses every failure into `("", 0.0)`, and `take` interprets that value as "the claim has lapsed". Concretely: agent B holds `refs/ddflow/claims/X` with `expires = now + 3600`. Agent A calls `take(...)`; A's root-commit push is correctly rejected as non-fast-forward; `_remote_sha` succeeds and returns B's sha `cur`; then `_read` runs `git fetch --no-tags <remote> refs/ddflow/claims/X`, which times out (the `TIMEOUT_S = 30` fetch is a data-transfer, and can time out on a slow/lossy link even though the earlier small `ls-remote` succeeded) and returns `("", 0.0)`. Back in `take`, `owner == holder` is false but `lapses <= time.time()` is `0.0 <= time.time()` → true, so A issues `git push --force-with-lease=<ref>:<cur>` at the sha B still holds, that push succeeds, and A returns `Result("ok", ...)` while B's live, unexpired claim is silently overwritten. This directly contradicts the module docstring ("`unavailable` ... is never treated as success"): a fetch failure or a claim message that `_parse` cannot read (missing/malformed `expires:` line ⇒ `0.0`) is treated as "expired" and grants the lock. The `_read` result needs a distinct failure signal (or `take` must check it) so a failed read refuses the claim instead of force-taking over.

chunk_findings.detail: The encoder is not injective for code points above U+00FF, because `f"%{ord(c):02x}"` emits more than two hex digits and is not prefixed by a length. `ord("€") = 0x20AC` ⇒ `%20ac`, while `" ac"` (space + `a` + `c`) ⇒ `%20` + `ac` ⇒ `%20ac` as well. Thus `ref_name("€") == ref_name(" ac") == "refs/ddflow/claims/%20ac"`: claiming item `"€"` makes the module report `held` for the entirely different item `" ac"` (and vice versa), so the docstring's guarantee that "ids stay distinct" is false. Any escaping scheme that must be collision-free needs a delimiter/prefix (e.g. encode the encoded byte length, or also escape a separator) so the escape sequence cannot be produced by a literal character.

chunk_findings.detail: `drop` never checks who holds the ref: it reads the current sha and force-with-lease deletes whatever is at that sha. Input/interleaving: A claims with a short TTL and then stalls past it; B observes the lapse, takes over (B's commit becomes `cur`); A resumes and performs its normal release, calling `drop(...)`. `drop` re-reads `cur` (now B's commit), the lease matches, and B's valid, unexpired claim is deleted, so the "mutual exclusion" the feature promises is gone. Note the asymmetry with `renew`, which does compare `owner != holder`; `drop` has no holder parameter at all, so no caller can perform a safe release through the public API.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/claimref.py:137-147 (`drop`)

chunk_findings.detail: `_make_commit` is documented/used as fallible (`take` wraps it in `try/except Exception` because "any local git failure means cannot claim remotely"), but `renew` calls it bare at line 129. If `git commit-tree` fails (check=True raising), `renew` propagates the exception instead of returning `Result("unavailable", ...)`, violating the module contract that "every function returns a `Result`" and turning a transient local git error into a crash in the heartbeat path.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_remote_drop(log, item_id)` is invoked unconditionally whenever the *local* transition succeeds in `release()` (line ~572) and `expire()` (line ~596), and it takes only `item_id` — no holder, no expected-value. It therefore cannot be a compare-and-swap: whatever ref `CR.drop` finds at `refs/ddflow/claims/<id>` is deleted, even if it is currently held by *another clone*.

Concrete failure: clone A has a lease record for X in remote mode. A crashes/the lease lapses, A's remote TTL elapses, and clone B wins the CAS and now legitimately holds X (remote ref written, B's local lease acquired). A's recovery still has the stale X lease entry and calls `expire(log, "X")` (or an operator calls `release(log, "X")`; release explicitly does not require the caller to be the holder). `_transition` succeeds locally, `done` is True, and `_remote_drop` deletes B's freshly-written ref. B continues to renew/heartbeat locally believing it holds X, while clone C can now `_remote_take` X successfully — two clones hold the same item, exactly the split-brain `[flow].claims = "remote"` exists to prevent. The only "protection" is the sentence "a ref we fail to delete lapses" — but here the delete *succeeds*, and it succeeds against the wrong owner. The drop must be conditional on the ref still naming the same holder the local lease transitioned (or on `CR.drop` taking the expected holder so it can CAS-delete), otherwise `expire`/`release` of a lapsed lease silently evicts the current remote holder.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases.py:371 (`_remote_drop`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The remote claim's expiry and the local lease's expiry are now computed from two different clocks, and the remote one is always the earlier. `acquire` evaluates `time.time()` *before* calling `_remote_take`, and `_remote_take` writes the remote ref with `now + cfg.lease.ttl_s`. `_acquire_locked` then captures its own `now = time.time()` *after* `_remote_take` has returned (the docstring itself says this can be up to six git subprocesses at 30 s each, i.e. ~180 s, plus however long the process then waits for the log append lock) and records the local lease with that later `now`. So the remote ref always expires `take_duration + lock_wait` before the local lease does.

Concrete case: `[flow].claims = "remote"`, `lease.ttl_s = 300`, and a `_remote_take` that takes 120 s. The remote ref is written with expiry `t+300`; `_acquire_locked` records the local lease with expiry `t+120+300 = t+420`. At `t+310` the remote ref is expired but the first clone's local lease is still valid (and its grace period hasn't even started). A second clone on its own log calls `acquire`, `_remote_take` sees the expired ref and takes it `"fresh"`, its own local checks pass (separate log), and it records a lease — for the next ~110 s (plus `grace_s`) both clones hold the same item, which is exactly the silent split-brain this setting exists to prevent. Because the first clone's lease is a one-shot (acquire → work → release), no renewal covers the gap; the window is reopened on every acquisition.

Before this change `_remote_take` was called inside `_acquire_locked` with that function's `now`, so the remote ref and the local lease expired together and the remote could never lapse while the local lease was still considered held. The fix is to derive the remote expiry from the same `now` that `_acquire_locked` will use for the local lease (e.g. pass the timestamp down, or re-`take` with the local `now` once the lease is recorded).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases.py: acquire (`_remote_take(..., time.time())`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The changed call passes only the holder string (`owner[0]`) to `_remote_drop`, but the remote ref is a single per-item ref whose content can only be compared by holder. When the same holder has held the item twice — exactly the B191 case called out in the unchanged comment immediately above the payload lambda — a late release or expiry of the first claim will see the remote ref still held by that same holder (the successor’s claim) and delete it.

Concrete input: take T1 for holder `"ghost"` with a lapsed expiry, then take T1 again for the same holder `"ghost"` with a future expiry so the remote ref now belongs to the new claim, then invoke the local release/expire path that ends the first claim. The payload captures `lease.holder` as `"ghost"`, `_remote_drop` sees the current remote ref’s holder is `"ghost"` and drops it, leaving the successor’s claim unprotected. The added test only exercises a different successor holder (`"agent-b"`), so it does not catch this same-holder successor case.

chunk_findings.detail:
When `cfg.flow.claims == "remote"` and `_holds_live(...)` is true, `acquire` now only calls `_remote_renew(...)` and never `_remote_take(...)`. But `_holds_live` consults **local** state only:

```python
it = _decide_from(log)[0].items.get(item_id)
lease = it.lease if it else None
return bool(lease and lease.holder == holder and not lease.expired(...))
```

So it can be true while the remote claim is gone. That is exactly the state the change's own comment describes for an outage ("it lapses at its expiry and the next heartbeat re-takes it"): the heartbeat keeps extending the local lease while `_remote_renew` cannot reach the remote, so the remote claim lapses and re-taking is a separate step. Once the remote is reachable again, calling `acquire(X)` finds `_holds_live` true, `_remote_renew` finds no live claim of ours to extend and returns falsy (no "lost" holder), and the code falls through to `_acquire_locked` and reports success *without ever re-establishing the remote claim*. Previously `acquire` unconditionally did `took = _remote_take(...)`, which claims an absent remote lease. Concrete input: `claims="remote"`, local lease for `X` held by us and unexpired, remote lease absent (but remote reachable) → `acquire(X)` returns success with no remote lock held; a second agent can then take the free remote lease and also succeed, so both agents believe they own `X`. The routing branch needs to distinguish "remote still ours" from "remote absent" (e.g., still call `_remote_take` when the renew finds nothing, only tolerating an unreachable-remote error).

Concrete case: an old item whose `item.completed` event has no `ledger` field, later followed by an `item.updated` that rewrites its title — `build` returns `reconstructed: True` and `requirement_changed_after: False`, even though the requirement demonstrably changed after completion. The check should compare `item_digest(it)` (completion-time) against `item_digest(now)`, not against `stored.get("req")`.

chunk_findings.detail: The test-detection regex misses the common `*.test.*` / `*.spec.*` file naming used by JS/TS projects. `_TEST` only matches a `tests/`/`spec/` path segment, a `test_` prefix ending at a `/` boundary, or a trailing `_test.<ext>`; a file named `src/foo.test.ts` (or `foo.spec.ts`) matches none of the three alternatives, so `search` returns `None`. Given a landing commit that changes `src/foo.test.ts` and nothing else, `git_facts` records `tests: []`, and `summary` consequently reports `tests: 0`, i.e. it states that the landing changed no tests when it did — directly contradicting the module's stated purpose of recording "which of them are tests."
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ledger.py:25 (`_TEST`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new alternative `\.(test|spec)\.[a-z]+$` matches *any* extension after `.test.`/`.spec.`, not just JavaScript/TypeScript test files as the change description ("js test names") implies. Previously `_TEST` only matched a `tests/`/`spec/` directory, a `test_` basename, or a `_test.<ext>` suffix, so a file like `openapi.spec.yaml` was correctly *not* classified as a test; now it is. Reproduce with a repo containing a non-test spec/config file such as `openapi.spec.yaml`, `schema.spec.json`, or `pkg.spec.py`: after this change `_TEST.search("openapi.spec.yaml")` is truthy, so `fact_files` puts it in the `tests` list and the ledger reports `tests among them 1` for a change that contains no test at all. This is not merely cosmetic: the ledger's `tests` count is exactly what downstream test-presence checks/gates read, so a pure config/spec edit can now satisfy a "the change includes tests" condition. The intent was to catch `.test.js`/`.spec.ts`-style names; constraining the final extension to the JS/TS family (e.g. `\.(test|spec)\.[cm]?[jt]sx?$`) would catch those without sweeping in unrelated `.spec.<ext>` files.

chunk_findings.detail: The new filter drops every path beginning with `.ddflow/` from the ledger's record of what a landing changed, and this filter is applied unconditionally to the ledger that both `ddflow show` (README: "files and tests the landing changed") and the new `ddflow verify` feature consume. The comment asserts `.ddflow/` is only queue bookkeeping, but the same comment admits `.ddflow/` holds *config*, and ddflow's rules/config are exactly the kind of artifact a legitimate task can change. Concrete input: a task whose declared/deliverable file is `.ddflow/<something>` (e.g. a rule or config file) that lands by modifying only that path. After this change the hunk yields `files == []`, `files_total == 0` even though `files_known` is still set `True`, so `ddflow show <id>` reports a landing that changed no files, contradicting the documented output, and any re-derivation built on the ledger (the "declared files exist"/"files survived" claims that `verify` is supposed to re-check) has a blind spot: a subsequent deletion of that `.ddflow/`-prefixed landed file is invisible to the survival check, so `ddflow verify <id>` can return success for a task whose declared file no longer exists. A narrower exclusion (or preserving a separate count/flag for bookkeeping-only paths) would avoid conflating "the landing changed only bookkeeping" with "the landing changed nothing the ledger can vouch for".

chunk_findings.detail: `_git_ok` returns `None` when the git call could not be made at all (`except Exception: return None`; the 60s timeout is explicitly passed, so a slow/timed-out call is an anticipated failure). `_landed` honours that for the existence probe (`exists = _git_ok(...); if exists is None: return UNKNOWN`), but the branch loop only does `if _git_ok(repo, "merge-base", "--is-ancestor", sha, b):`, so `None` is indistinguishable from "not an ancestor". Concrete case: a large repo where `cat-file -e <sha>` succeeds but `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> main` exceeds 60s (or subsection of git raises for any other reason). The loop falls through and the function returns `Claim("landed", FAIL, "<sha> exists but is on none of main")`, `Report.failed` becomes True, and `ddflow verify` exits 1 — accusing a completion that did land of never landing, when in fact git simply could not be asked. Same repo, same helper, same unanswered question as the `cat-file` path that correctly yields `UNKNOWN`, so the two outcomes contradict each other and the FAIL is not a check that failed.

chunk_findings.detail: The intent is "commit landed on the integration branch". For a gitflow repo the integration branch is `cfg.flow.develop_branch` (develop); `default_branch(repo)` is the release branch (main/master). But `_landed` builds `branches = [default_branch(repo)]` and merely *appends* `develop` when `cfg.flow.model == "gitflow"`, then returns `OK` if the recorded commit is an ancestor of *any* branch in that list. So a completion whose commit is only on `main` (e.g. a hotfix committed directly on main in the gitflow hotfix flow and not yet back-merged into develop) is reported `Claim("landed", OK, "<sha> is on main")`; `verdict` then yields "holds" and the CLI exits 0, even though the change was never integrated. The commit-exists test (`cat-file -e`) will succeed for such a commit, and `merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> main` returns 0, so the `develop` check is never even needed. In gitflow the landing check should be restricted to the integration (develop) branch rather than accepting the release branch as equivalent.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/verify.py:_landed

chunk_findings.detail: The `FAIL`-with-no-claims branch is evaluated *before* the `if c.json:` branch, so it short-circuits the JSON wire body that the function's own module docstring promises ("Same call, same wire body as the `ddflow_verify` MCP tool"). Concretely: run `ddflow --json verify <id>` for any input where `api.verify` returns `exit == FAIL` with an empty `claims` list (the exact class of failure this branch exists to handle — e.g. id not found / repo not a git repo / nothing to recompute). The command prints `out.reason` to stderr and returns `FAIL` without writing anything to stdout, so a machine consumer that parses stdout (e.g. `ddflow --json verify "$id" | jq`) receives empty output with exit 1, whereas the non-`--json` path at least has stderr and the MCP tool would have returned a body. `out.data` in this case still has `item`/`verdict` and would serialize fine, so the early return is only needed for the human-readable reason; it should come after the `c.json` check (or the `c.json` check should be first) so the JSON contract is honored for all exits.

chunk_findings.detail: The new description string is malformed: it ends with "(the CLI's `--agent})" — an unbalanced open paren, a stray closing brace, and an unterminated backtick — and it drops the clause that told callers *which* tools accept the parameter ("every OTHER tool takes it; same name rules"). chunk_findings.detail: `_declared` assumes a declared exact path that is absent from `tracked` is "never created" unless the landing itself touched it (`gone`). That binary is unsound: the landing need not touch every declared path, and a declared path can pre-exist, go untouched by the landing, then be removed by an unrelated later commit. Concretely, with `requirement.globs = ["pkg/a.py", "pkg/b.py"]` (both non-wildcard, both pre-existing), a landing that touched only `pkg/a.py` (`done.files = ["pkg/a.py", ...]`), and a later commit deleting `pkg/b.py`: `exact = ["pkg/a.py","pkg/b.py"]`, `tracked` no longer contains `pkg/b.py`, and `landed` does not either, so `never = ["pkg/b.py"]` and the claim returns `FAIL "declared but never created: pkg/b.py"`, driving `Report.verdict` to `does not hold`. The file did exist and was removed afterwards; the code has no way to distinguish that from never-created, so per the module's own rule ("Could not tell is never reported as ok") this should be `WARN`/`UNKNOWN`, not a hard FAIL. The same misclassification fires when `done.files_known` is False (reconstructed ledger, `landed` empty): a declared path that was created and later deleted is reported as "declared but never created" instead of `UNKNOWN`, because `landed` is empty rather than unknown.

chunk_findings.detail: The new filter drops every path beginning with `.ddflow/` from the ledger's record of what a landing changed, and this filter is applied unconditionally to the ledger that both `ddflow show` (README: "files and tests the landing changed") and the new `ddflow verify` feature consume. The comment asserts `.ddflow/` is only queue bookkeeping, but the same comment admits `.ddflow/` holds *config*, and ddflow's rules/config are exactly the kind of artifact a legitimate task can change. Concrete input: a task whose declared/deliverable file is `.ddflow/<something>` (e.g. a rule or config file) that lands by modifying only that path. After this change the hunk yields `files == []`, `files_total == 0` even though `files_known` is still set `True`, so `ddflow show <id>` reports a landing that changed no files, contradicting the documented output, and any re-derivation built on the ledger (the "declared files exist"/"files survived" claims that `verify` is supposed to re-check) has a blind spot: a subsequent deletion of that `.ddflow/`-prefixed landed file is invisible to the survival check, so `ddflow verify <id>` can return success for a task whose declared file no longer exists. A narrower exclusion (or preserving a separate count/flag for bookkeeping-only paths) would avoid conflating "the landing changed only bookkeeping" with "the landing changed nothing the ledger can vouch for".
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ledger.py:60 (`files` filter)

chunk_findings.detail: `_git_ok` returns `None` when the git call could not be made at all (`except Exception: return None`; the 60s timeout is explicitly passed, so a slow/timed-out call is an anticipated failure). `_landed` honours that for the existence probe (`exists = _git_ok(...); if exists is None: return UNKNOWN`), but the branch loop only does `if _git_ok(repo, "merge-base", "--is-ancestor", sha, b):`, so `None` is indistinguishable from "not an ancestor". Concrete case: a large repo where `cat-file -e <sha>` succeeds but `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> main` exceeds 60s (or subsection of git raises for any other reason). The loop falls through and the function returns `Claim("landed", FAIL, "<sha> exists but is on none of main")`, `Report.failed` becomes True, and `ddflow verify` exits 1 — accusing a completion that did land of never landing, when in fact git simply could not be asked. Same repo, same helper, same unanswered question as the `cat-file` path that correctly yields `UNKNOWN`, so the two outcomes contradict each other and the FAIL is not a check that failed.

chunk_findings.detail: The `FAIL`-without-claims guard returns before the `c.json` branch, so the structured wire body promised by the module docstring ("Same call, same wire body as the `ddflow_verify` MCP tool") is never emitted in `--json` mode. Given a response where `verify` returns `exit == FAIL` and `out.data` has no/empty `"claims"` (the exact case this branch exists to handle — e.g. verification fails before any claim can be computed), running `ddflow verify <id> --json` prints only `out.reason` to stderr and leaves stdout empty; a caller doing `json.loads(stdout)` gets an empty document instead of the body that `out.body(("item","verdict","claims"))` would have produced. The `c.json` branch should be reached (or the reason included in the body) for this case as well, so that JSON mode always emits a parseable body.

chunk_findings.detail: `_ever_existed` runs `git log --all`, which walks *every* ref in the repository (all local branches, remotes, tags, stash), not the history the verified landing descends from. In the multi-task/worktree setting this tool runs in, consider task T1 whose landing sha `S` never creates `declared.py` (absent from T1's worktree), while a sibling branch `task/T2` does contain `declared.py`. `_tracked` (current worktree) excludes the path, so it lands in `absent`; `git log --all -- declared.py` finds T2's commit, so `_ever_existed` returns True, the path is put in `removed_later`, `never` is empty, and `_declared` returns WARN ("existed once but absent now") instead of FAIL ("declared but never created") — the exact false-plan failure the claim exists to catch. A later commit that adds then deletes the path also triggers this. Scoping the query to the landing commit (or its base), e.g. `git log <sha> -- path`, still recognizes a file that was created and removed *before* the task (the removal commit is an ancestor of the landing), while ignoring unrelated branches.

chunk_findings.detail: The scope is resolved with `st.descendants(phase)` *before* the guard `if phase and phase not in st.items:` runs, so the guard is downstream of the very lookup it is supposed to protect. With input `ddflow verify --phase does-not-exist`, execution reaches `st.descendants("does-not-exist")` with an id that is absent from `st.items`; any `descendants` implementation that resolves the argument through the item map (rather than scanning all items) raises `KeyError` there, and the function terminates with a traceback instead of reaching the intended `O.failed("verify.sweep", "no such phase ...")` at the next line. Swapping the two statements (validate `phase in st.items` first, then compute `scope`) removes the hazard and is the only reason the `no such phase` branch can be relied on.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/verify.py:37 (`verify_sweep`, `scope = st.descendants(phase) ...`)

chunk_findings.detail: `git log --grep` matches against the *entire* commit message (subject + body), and it is an unanchored substring match; `-F` only disables regex interpretation, it does not restrict the match to the subject line. So the helper can return a commit that does not have the recorded commit's subject at all, yet the caller prints "a commit with the same subject is (<hash>): history was rewritten since" and downgrades a genuine `FAIL` ("exists but is on none of ...") to a `WARN`. Concrete input: recorded commit subject is `Fix the login redirect bug`; the branch contains a different commit whose subject is `Fix the login redirect bug in mobile` (superstring) or whose body merely contains the line `See also: Fix the login redirect bug`. In either case `git log -1 --format=%H -F --grep=Fix the login redirect bug <branch>` returns that commit, so a commit that was never rewritten/landed is reported as a rewritten twin. To actually match the subject the command would need the subject line isolated/anchored (e.g. filter `%s` per commit or anchor the pattern), not a message-wide `--grep`.

chunk_findings.detail: `_MARK` is still the four-entry map `{"ok", "warn", "fail", "unknown"}`, but this change makes the sweep capable of producing a problem whose status is the new `cannot-tell` label (the intent explicitly states "imported completions are cannot-tell"). `_sweep` renders every problem through `_MARK[p['status']]`, so the first time `ddflow verify --all` ranks a done task whose imported completion yields a `cannot-tell` problem entry, the dict lookup raises `KeyError: 'cannot-tell'` and the whole sweep aborts with a traceback instead of printing the row. The same lookup is used for single-item claims in `_one`, so `ddflow verify <id>` on an imported completion hits it too. The change needed to add the `cannot-tell` status to `_MARK` (or fall back for unknown statuses); because `_MARK` is untouched context, the new status is unrenderable.

chunk_findings.detail:
`verify_sweep` resolves the phase scope before it validates that the phase exists:

```python
scope = st.descendants(phase) if phase else None
if phase and phase not in st.items:
    return O.failed("verify.sweep", f"no such phase {phase!r}", phase=phase)
```

`st.descendants(phase)` computes the subtree rooted at `phase` and therefore has to resolve `phase` in `st.items` (that is exactly why the very next line checks `phase not in st.items`). For the input `ddflow verify --phase no-such-phase`, `phase` is not a key of `st.items`, so the call on the first line raises `KeyError` before the guard on the third line can fire; the command escapes with an unhandled traceback instead of the intended `no such phase 'no-such-phase'` failure. The guard is dead for the only case it exists to handle — the existence check must precede, or wrap, the `descendants` call (e.g. look up `st.items.get(phase)` first and only then compute the scope).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/verify.py (verify_sweep: `scope = st.descendants(phase)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new rule set claims (in its own docstring) "every required gate PASSED", but the `required_bad` comprehension filters with `if g in pipeline and ...`, so a gate listed in `cfg.gates.required` that is not part of the `pipeline` argument is never examined. This is also a regression: the old code had `missing = [g for g in cfg.gates.required if g not in gates]`, which failed unconditionally for any required gate absent from the ledger. Concrete input: `cfg.gates.required = ["security"]`, `cfg.gates.require_outcome` false, `pipeline = ["lint", "tests"]`, `gates = {"lint": {...}, "tests": {...}}` (both passed). `silent` is empty (security is not in `pipeline`), `required_bad` is empty (`g in pipeline` is false), `unreasoned` is empty, so `_gates` returns `Claim("gates", OK, "2 gate(s) recorded, none blocking")` for a completion that never ran a required gate — previously this returned FAIL. The same filter also corrupts the note at the bottom: with `gates = {"security": {"outcome": "failed"}}` and the same config, the failed *required* gate falls through to `notes.append(f"failed but not required: ...")`, so verify reports a required gate as "not required" and downgrades a genuine gate failure from FAIL to WARN.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/verify.py:_gates (`required_bad` comprehension)

chunk_findings.detail: `add_verify_parser` puts `--file-bugs` on the shared `verify` parser, and its help text ("file a bug for each completion that does not hold") applies to the subcommand as a whole. However `cmd_verify` dispatches `if a.id: return _one(a, c)`, and `_one` calls `verify(c.repo, a.id)` with no `file_bugs` argument (and never passes `a.file_bugs` anywhere). So `ddflow verify T-42 --file-bugs` parses successfully, runs the single-item path, files nothing, and emits no warning that the flag was ignored. The user gets exit 0/1 as if bugs had been handled, while no bug record is created. Either `_one` must forward `a.file_bugs` to the api (if the single-item call supports it) or the flag must be rejected/documented as sweep-only; silently swallowing a user-supplied write-performing flag is the defect.

Concrete input: `cfg.gates.required = ["security"]`, `cfg.gates.require_outcome` false, `pipeline = ["lint", "tests"]`, `gates = {"lint": {...}, "tests": {...}}` (both passed). `silent` is empty (security is not in `pipeline`), `required_bad` is empty (`g in pipeline` is false), `unreasoned` is empty, so `_gates` returns `Claim("gates", OK, "2 gate(s) recorded, none blocking")` for a completion that never ran a required gate — previously this returned FAIL. The same filter also corrupts the note at the bottom: with `gates = {"security": {"outcome": "failed"}}` and the same config, the failed *required* gate falls through to `notes.append(f"failed but not required: ...")`, so verify reports a required gate as "not required" and downgrades a genuine gate failure from FAIL to WARN.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/verify.py:_gates (`required_bad` comprehension)

chunk_findings.detail: `add_verify_parser` puts `--file-bugs` on the shared `verify` parser, and its help text ("file a bug for each completion that does not hold") applies to the subcommand as a whole. However `cmd_verify` dispatches `if a.id: return _one(a, c)`, and `_one` calls `verify(c.repo, a.id)` with no `file_bugs` argument (and never passes `a.file_bugs` anywhere). So `ddflow verify T-42 --file-bugs` parses successfully, runs the single-item path, files nothing, and emits no warning that the flag was ignored. The user gets exit 0/1 as if bugs had been handled, while no bug record is created. Either `_one` must forward `a.file_bugs` to the api (if the single-item call supports it) or the flag must be rejected/documented as sweep-only; silently swallowing a user-supplied write-performing flag is the defect.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/verify.py:cmd_verify / _one

chunk_findings.detail:
The default/glob branch ranks files by lexicographic comparison of the *full repo‑relative path*, and the docstring asserts this is "how a default pytest run orders files." That is not the same order pytest actually uses: pytest's directory collector sorts each directory's entries by *basename* and then recurses, so a directory whose name is a prefix of a sibling file's name is entered **before** that file, whereas string comparison of the full paths puts the file first because `'.'` (0x2E) < `'/'` (0x2F).

Concrete failure: a repo with `tests/test_a.py` (the victim) and `tests/test_a/test_z.py` (a polluter). pytest sorts the entries of `tests/` as `test_a` (dir) < `test_a.py` (file), so it collects and runs `tests/test_a/test_z.py` before `tests/test_a.py` — the victim really is polluted by it. Here `found` is `["tests/test_a.py", "tests/test_a/test_z.py"]` after `sorted(...)` (the file sorts first), and `f < victim_file` drops `tests/test_a/test_z.py` because `"tests/test_a/test_z.py" > "tests/test_a.py"`. `candidates_before` therefore returns `[]`, `is_bisect` finds no candidates, and the tool reports "nothing to report / no polluter" for a victim that genuinely fails only in full-suite order. The same inversion occurs for any sibling file named `<dir>.py` next to directory `<dir>/`.

chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/bisect.py:48 (`candidates_before`, `return [f for f in found if f < victim_file]`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The change adds four queue-related attributes to `PRInfo` (`queue`, `queue_position`, `queue_state`, `queue_known`), but `event_data()` serializes only the first three. `queue_known` is the one attribute that carries the distinction the code's own comment says must be preserved: "False when the queue could not be ASKED (rate limit, network, auth): 'not queued' would then be a guess, and a guess that reads as an ejection is worse than none."

Concrete failure: PR #7 is open and advertised as `queue="queued"` in one snapshot. The next poll's `gh pr view` succeeds but `_queue()` returns `None` (rate limit / network), so `_info()` sets `info.queue_known = False` and `info.queue` stays at the dataclass default `""`. Any consumer that reads the serialized `event_data()` payload (the only place the new queue fields are surfaced) receives `{"queue": "", "queue_position": 0, "queue_state": ""}`, byte-identical to "definitely not queued", and the `queue_known=False` signal that was supposed to suppress this reading never crosses the boundary. A sweep comparing snapshots therefore sees "queued" → "" and concludes the request was ejected from the queue — precisely the false ejection the `queue_known` field was introduced to prevent. Either `queue_known` must be emitted alongside the other queue fields, or the `queue*` fields must not be emitted when the queue was not asked.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/forge.py:87-89 (`PRInfo.event_data`)

chunk_findings.detail: `_report_queue` classifies an item as ejected purely from `was_queued and info.state == "open"`; it never consults `info.queue_known`, even though its sibling `_waiting` (same diff) explicitly treats `not info.queue_known` as its own state ("the merge queue could not be read, so ddflow will not merge this until it can"). When the queue probe fails transiently, `info.queue` is false and `info.state` is still the PR's real state, so for an item that a previous sync stored as queued (`was_queued` true), the `elif` fires and `rep.changes` gets a `queue_ejected` entry with the text "ejected from the merge queue without merging (the queue's own checks failed, or someone dequeued it) … Fix it and it is queued again once approved and green." The user is told the PR was thrown out of the queue, and told to re-approve/re-green it, when in fact the queue simply could not be read and the PR may still be sitting in it — exactly the situation `_waiting` goes out of its way to report as "unknown". The `elif` needs `info.queue_known` (or an explicit unknown branch) before claiming an ejection.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/flow.py `_report_queue`

chunk_findings.detail: The new guard moves `--file-bugs` handling into an "if `a.id`" rejection, but the fall-through path for `--file-bugs` without an id (and without `--all`/`--phase`) is left to the pre-existing `if a.all or a.phase:` branch, which is false, so `cmd_verify` returns `None` implicitly and exits 0 while doing nothing. If the CLI declares `--file-bugs` as a valid verify flag (the intent describes it as a sweep flag, so a sweep invocation without `--all`/`--phase` is plausible), then `verify --file-bugs` silently reports success without running any file-bug check. This is only reachable if the CLI validation does not make `--all`/`--phase` mandatory whenever `--file-bugs` is given; if such validation exists elsewhere, this is not a defect.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/verify.py:75

chunk_findings.detail:
The change advertises (and the change intent states) that sweep-only flags are *rejected* when a single task is verified, but the MCP handler does the opposite: it silently drops them. The lambda is

```
_api().verify_item(repo, a["id"], agent=agent) if a.get("id") else _api().verify_sweep(...)
```

so when `id` is present, `phase`, `limit` and `file_bugs` are never forwarded to `verify_item` and no guard can run. Concretely, calling the tool with `{"id": "T1", "file_bugs": true}` returns a normal single-item verification (and `payload` is now `""`, so no bug was filed and nothing signals the flag was ignored), instead of the rejection the rest of the change requires. Because `verify_item` is only ever handed `repo`/`id`/`agent` here, there is no path in this surface by which the "sweep flags rejected on a single task" rule can be enforced; the caller gets a success response that looks like the flag was honored.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:1441-1456 (ddflow_verify api lambda)
